source: Terms used in the three Earth-as-a-planet decks (U1). Adapted from OpenStax Astronomy 2e sections 8.1, 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
translationStatus: English only for now. Translations follow in a separate pass once the cohort languages are confirmed; the language selector stays off this page until then.

terms.plain: How much mass is packed into a given amount of space. Two rocks the same size can have very different densities.
terms.note: The whole argument for Earth having a metal core starts here: the planet as a whole is denser than the rock on its surface.

terms.plain: A wave of energy that travels through the Earth, usually made by an earthquake.
terms.note: Seismic waves are the only tool we have for looking inside the planet. Everything in deck 1 rests on them.

terms.plain: A region of Earth's surface where a particular kind of seismic wave never arrives after an earthquake.
terms.note: A place where nothing arrives is evidence. The shadow zone is how the liquid outer core was found.

terms.plain: The thin outer rock layer of a planet. On Earth it is a few kilometers thick under the oceans and much thicker under the continents.
terms.note: Only 0.3 percent of Earth's mass, and the only part anyone has ever sampled directly.

terms.plain: The thick rock layer between a planet's crust and its core. On Earth it reaches down about 2,900 km.
terms.note: Solid, but it can deform slowly under pressure, which is what lets it move over long periods.

terms.plain: The dense metal center of a planet. Earth's has a liquid outer part and a solid inner part.
terms.note: Mostly iron and nickel. The liquid outer part is what generates the magnetic field.

terms.plain: A dark, dense volcanic rock. It makes up most of the ocean floor.
A lighter-colored, less dense rock. It makes up most of the continents.
terms.note: Continents float higher than ocean floor because granite is less dense than basalt.

terms.plain: The sorting of a planet's material by density while the planet is molten: heavy material sinks to the middle, light material rises to the top.
terms.note: A planet has to be hot enough to be liquid for this to happen. A planet that never melted would be the same all the way through.

terms.plain: A process that generates a magnetic field from moving, electrically conducting fluid. In a planet, that fluid is liquid metal in the core.
terms.note: Say "process", not "thing". A dynamo needs the motion to continue; if the core stops circulating, the field goes away.

terms.plain: The region of magnetic influence around a magnet or a planet, and the strength and direction of that influence at each point.
The region around a planet where the planet's own magnetic field is stronger than the magnetic field carried by the solar wind.
terms.note: Earth's reaches about 60,000 km on the day side and is stretched into a long tail on the night side.

terms.plain: The constant stream of charged particles blowing outward from the Sun in all directions.
terms.note: This is what stripped Mars. It is the thing a magnetosphere protects you from.

terms.plain: Two zones of high-energy charged particles trapped inside Earth's magnetic field.
terms.note: Found by Explorer 1 in 1958, the first American satellite. Named for the scientist whose instrument detected them.

terms.plain: The first atmosphere a planet has, made of the light gases it captured from the cloud it formed in: mostly hydrogen and helium.
terms.note: Earth lost its primary atmosphere. Jupiter kept its own, because it is far more massive and far colder.

terms.plain: The replacement atmosphere a planet builds from gas released out of its own interior.
terms.note: Earth's second atmosphere came out of volcanoes. Our current one is arguably a third, because life rebuilt it.

terms.plain: The release of gas that was trapped inside a planet's rock out to its surface, mostly through volcanoes.
A unit of pressure, defined as exactly 100 kilopascals. It was chosen because it is close to the pressure of Earth's atmosphere at sea level.
terms.note: Close to, not equal to. Earth's actual sea-level pressure is about 101 kPa, so about 1.01 bar. Astronomers round it to 1 bar and use that as the planetary yardstick.

terms.plain: A metric unit of pressure, written kPa. Earth's sea-level air pressure is about 101 kPa.
terms.note: 1 bar = 100 kPa exactly. Pick one unit for your framework column and stay in it; do not convert halfway down the table.

terms.plain: A mineral that contains carbon and oxygen bonded together, formed when dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with rock. Limestone is made of it.
terms.note: Most of the carbon dioxide Earth's volcanoes released is now locked in carbonate rock, not in the air.

terms.plain: A layered mound built up in shallow water by mats of microbes trapping sediment.
terms.note: Among the oldest fossil evidence of life on Earth, and the oldest you can look at in a photograph. The well-accepted ones are about 3.5 billion years old.

terms.plain: A living thing too small to see without a microscope, such as a bacterium.
terms.note: For most of Earth's history, microbes were the only life there was.

terms.plain: The process by which some living things use sunlight to build sugar out of carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as waste.
terms.note: The oxygen in the air you are breathing is a waste product. That framing is worth sitting with.

terms.plain: A group of bacteria that can photosynthesize. Older texts call them blue-green algae, but they are not algae.
terms.note: OpenStax uses the older name. The organism is the same.

terms.plain: A molecule made of three oxygen atoms, written O3. It forms high in the atmosphere and absorbs ultraviolet light.
terms.note: Ordinary oxygen is O2. Ozone is a different molecule with different behavior.

terms.plain: Light with more energy than the violet end of the visible range. You cannot see it, and it damages living tissue.
terms.note: Often shortened to UV.

terms.plain: A state that has not settled down: gases that should have finished reacting with each other are still both present.
terms.note: Lovelock's whole 1965 argument, from Unit 0 Block 2. Disequilibrium needs something to keep maintaining it.

terms.plain: Something you can measure about a planet that would be hard to explain unless something living were there.
terms.note: The oxygen-and-methane pair is the standard example. It is Hitchcock and Lovelock's, from 1967, two years after the paper you read in Unit 0. A biosignature is a strong hint, never a proof.

terms.plain: A bowl-shaped hollow left where an object from space struck a planet or moon.
The wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil by water, ice, wind, or gravity.
terms.note: Unit 2 is built on this. Here it matters because it is one of the reasons Earth has so few visible craters.

terms.plain: The slow movement of the large sections that Earth's crust is broken into, driven by motion in the mantle below.
terms.note: Unit 3 covers this properly. Here you only need one consequence: crust gets recycled, so old surfaces do not survive.

terms.plain: A dense metal that is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids.
terms.note: Finding a lot of it in a thin worldwide clay layer is what made scientists predict a large impact before the crater was found.

terms.plain: An event in which a large share of the species alive on Earth die out in a short period of geological time.
An asteroid or comet whose orbit brings it close to Earth's orbit.
terms.note: Often shortened to NEO. Surveys track them; the DART mission tested whether one could be pushed off course.
